new_statements.quote: There are two common stress patterns in Wooi, i.e. penultimate stress and syllable final stem stress. Penultimate stress is a dominant pattern over the syllable final stem stress. [...] 2.4.1. Penultimate stress. The dominant stress pattern in Wooi is for primary stress to occur on the penultimate syllable. Penultimate stress is then considered as the default stress pattern in Wooi. This stress pattern may occur in phonological and morphological words. Morphological words count all pre-verbal affixations as stress dependent; while post-verbal element are stress independent. [p. 52:] The second stress pattern in Wooi is the syllabic-final stress pattern. [...] Some nouns, mainly disyllabic words, have stress on the final syllable. These words ends with the high front vowel /i/.
new_statements.citation: Sawaki, Yusuf Willem. 2016. A grammar of Wooi: An Austronesian language of Yapen Island, Western New Guinea. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl:1885/136851).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic and by default falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (examples [ˈma:.nu] 'house', [kŏ.ˈri:.si] 'one', [ßă.ră.ˈpe:.ma] 'wing'); subject and applicative prefixes are inside the stress domain, the object enclitic =i is outside it, so stress stays on the penult of prefix+stem. Stressed vowels are lengthened and have higher intensity. A minority lexical/morphological class has stem-final stress: disyllabic nouns ending in /i/ ([ka.ˈmi:] 'stone'), inalienably possessed body-part nouns whose final syllable begins with a sonorant ([ßa.ˈra:] 'my hands', stress staying on the stem-final syllable under suffixation: [ßă.ˈra:.mu]), and perception verbs where stress falls on the verbalizer -ho ([rě.ˈho] 'I saw', [rě.mǔ.ˈho.i]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In polysyllabic (compound) words a less prominent secondary stress falls on the second syllable preceding the penultimate primary stress, e.g. [ˌma.rja.ˈra:.ro] 'river', [ˌta.ra.ˈkam.rěj] 'ear'; footnote 2 (p. 54) says secondary stress in words of more than four syllables needs further research.
new_statements.exceptions: Stem-final stress class (section 2.4.2): /i/-final disyllabic nouns, body-part nouns with sonorant-initial final syllable, -ho perception verbs; enclitic =i never stressed; diphthong nuclei not lengthened under stress. Author calls the whole analysis 'preliminary' and 'based on very limited data'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (morphological) word: prefixes count, enclitics do not. Evidence from citation forms with Praat measurements (duration, intensity) and spectrograms (Figs 2.1-2.4, Table 2.3 p. 32). Abstract (p. viii) states 'Stress is not phonemic.'
new_statements.identity_note: Sawaki writes the language name 'Wooi' (Glottolog/ISO 'Woi', wbw, woii1237); described variety is that of Wooi, Woinap and Yenuari villages at the western tip of Yapen Island — same languoid, no dialect split reported.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.4 'Basic stress patterns' (pp. 48-55): stress not phonemic; default/dominant pattern is primary stress on the penultimate syllable (pre-verbal prefixes count in the stress domain, enclitics do not); a second, minor pattern is stem-final stress (disyllabic nouns ending in /i/, inalienable body-part nouns with a sonorant-initial final syllable, and perception verbs with the verbalizer -ho); secondary stress two syllables before the primary in longer words; stressed vowels lengthen (Table 2.3, p. 32, with duration/intensity measurements and spectrograms).
